tldr: By generating search candidates along the tangent space of the constraint manifold and verifying them in parallel on the GPU, motion planning for high-dimensional, highly constrained dual-arm and humanoid tasks was accelerated by up to 11.25 times.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of PATACON. Each CUDA block dynamically selects a local tangent space (local linear approximation plane) from a shared bank, and candidate edges along the manifold are generated, projected, and validated in parallel on the GPU, achieving efficient bidirectional search.
overview:
When humanoids or dual-arm robots carry objects or maintain balance, they must continuously satisfy complex geometric constraints (equality constraints), such as closed-chain constraints holding an object with both hands or foot support constraints. In this kind of constrained motion planning, each time a search tree is extended, the candidate trajectory must be pulled back onto the target surface (constraint manifold) through "constraint projection." Solving this repeatedly becomes a major computational bottleneck.

Recently, massively parallel GPU planners such as cpRRTC have emerged. However, they still extend branches randomly in the unconstrained ambient space (ambient configuration space) and forcibly project deviating points back to the manifold. As a result, when the dimension grows and constraints become tighter, wasted projections surge, and search efficiency drops sharply.

To tackle this, the authors reasoned that extending branches along the tangent space, which reflects the local slope of the manifold, would drastically reduce unnecessary projections. Existing tangent space methods such as TB-RRT were designed for sequential execution and were hard to parallelize. In this work, the authors built a mechanism to share tangent space data across CUDA blocks, along with a scheme to generate multiple candidate edges at once from a single sample and validate them in parallel.

Evaluations across eight environments ranging from 7-DoF arms to 35-DoF humanoid whole-body planning showed that the proposed method shines brighter as dimensionality and constraint codimension increase, achieving up to an 11.25 times speedup and a 100% success rate compared to the existing GPU-parallel planner.
contributions: Integrated exploration guided by the local geometry of the constraint manifold (tangent space) with massively parallel GPU processing for the first time.
Proposed a "tangent-space bank" mechanism to share and reuse tangent spaces per search tree across multiple CUDA blocks.
Introduced Tangent-Guided Multi-Edge Projection (TGMP), generating multiple edges along the tangent direction from a single sample and nearest-neighbor query to validate them in batch on the GPU.

Demonstrated in benchmark experiments including humanoid whole-body planning that advantages over existing methods widen in higher dimensions and under tighter constraints, achieving up to an 11.25 times speedup.

sections.heading: Why is constrained planning heavy even with GPU parallelization?
sections.summary: In constrained motion planning, the overhead of constraint projection explodes as robot degrees of freedom and constraint tightness increase. Existing GPU-parallel methods blindly steer in the ambient space before projecting, causing efficiency to collapse on high-dimensional, highly constrained problems.
sections.details:
Dual-arm object transport and humanoid whole-body movements must satisfy not only joint limits and collision avoidance, but also kinematic constraints such as maintaining relative end-effector poses or keeping feet planted. These are formulated as nonlinear equality constraints, defining a low-dimensional "constraint manifold" embedded within a high-dimensional joint configuration space.

In sampling-based motion planning, on top of already heavy collision checking and nearest-neighbor searches, extending a tree incurs immense repeated numerical iterations for "constraint projection" to bring states back onto the manifold. In dynamic environments where obstacles and goals shift constantly, this planning latency is fatal for continuous replanning.

Recently, massively parallel planners like cpRRTC have emerged, assigning straight-line steering, projection, and collision checking to thread blocks on GPUs to achieve search times on the order of milliseconds. However, the fundamental search strategy remained unchanged. They still steer in random directions across the ambient space without considering the shape of the constraints, and then forcibly project candidates onto the manifold. This produces many wasted samples that barely make progress along the manifold after projection, squandering compute resources.

Meanwhile, steering along a local tangent space obtained from the null space of the Jacobian matrix has long been known to reduce deviations from the manifold and cut down projections (e.g., TB-RRT). However, building and managing tangent spaces adds overhead, making it difficult to leverage the raw power of parallel GPUs with purely sequential logic.

To break this bottleneck, this paper introduces PATACON (GPU-Parallel Tangent-Bundle RRT-Connect). By embedding tangent-space-guided exploration into massively parallel GPU processing and amortizing management costs across multiple candidate edges, it overcomes this fundamental challenge.

sections.heading: Prior wisdom for tracing manifolds and the barrier to parallelization
sections.summary: Constrained planning methods include numerical projection and tangent-space or local-chart approaches, but most rely on sequential CPU execution. Existing GPU-parallel methods remain limited to simple ambient-space extension, leaving tangent-space geometry largely unexplored on GPUs.
sections.details:
Sampling-based methods for constraints have a rich research history. Broadly, they fall into projection-based methods—such as randomized gradient descent, first-order Jacobian retraction, and CBiRRT, which pull out-of-manifold points back via numerical projection—and manifold/tangent-space methods like AtlasRRT and TB-RRT, which tile the space with local coordinate charts or tangent spaces and grow trees over them. However, these are fundamentally sequential algorithms that advance one node at a time on the CPU.

Recently, deep-learning approaches that learn constraint-satisfying latent spaces have emerged. Yet, they require extensive offline data collection and retraining, making it difficult to adapt flexibly to arbitrary constraint functions.

Another mainstream route to slash computation time is parallelization. Multi-threaded CPU search, SIMD vectorization (such as McVAMP), and GPU-based collision checking or trajectory optimization have been developed. More recently, pRRTC—which grows full RRT trees on the GPU—and its constrained extension cpRRTC achieved substantial speedups.

However, cpRRTC simply steers in ambient space and projects waypoints in parallel on the GPU. While parallelization reduces the cost per projection, it does not reduce the wasteful exploration that drifts off the manifold. Incorporating tangent spaces has been blocked by the overhead of building tangent spaces and running local nearest-neighbor searches, which hurts performance when naively combined. PATACON was specifically designed to resolve this dilemma.

sections.heading: Problem formulation: Finding a thin manifold hidden in configuration space
sections.summary: Within the robot configuration space $\mathcal{C}$, we address the constraint manifold $\mathcal{M}$ defined by equality constraints $h(q)=0$. Using an orthonormal null-space basis $N(q)$ of the Jacobian to represent tangent spaces, the goal is formulated as finding a safe, continuous, collision-free path.
sections.details:
Let the robot configuration space be $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, and let a robot configuration be $q \in \mathcal{C}$. Task kinematic constraints are given as a differentiable nonlinear equality constraint function $h(q) = 0$, where $h: \mathcal{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$. The set satisfying this constraint is the constraint manifold $\mathcal{M} = \{q \in \mathcal{C} \mid h(q) = 0\}$.

At regular points where the Jacobian matrix $J_h(q) = \partial h(q) / \partial q$ has full rank $m$, the local manifold dimension is $d = n - m$. The local tangent space (the flat space tangent to the manifold) is then given by:

$T_q \mathcal{M} = \{v \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid J_h(q) v = 0\}$

PATACON computes an orthonormal basis for this null space as a matrix $N(q) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, satisfying $J_h(q) N(q) = 0$ and $N(q)^\top N(q) = I_d$. This matrix $N(q)$ serves as a local coordinate system to explore freely inside the tangent space.

Furthermore, letting $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{free}}$ be the safe region free of self-collisions and environmental collisions, the feasible manifold to explore is defined as $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{free}} = \mathcal{M} \cap \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{free}}$. The objective is to find a continuous path $\sigma: [0, 1] \rightarrow \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{free}}$ connecting a given start state $q_{\mathrm{start}} \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{free}}$ and goal state $q_{\mathrm{goal}} \in \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{free}}$, such that every point strictly satisfies constraints, joint limits, and collision avoidance.

sections.heading: PATACON architecture: Shared tangent spaces and batch multi-edge validation
sections.summary: PATACON rests on two pillars: Tangent-Guided Sampling (TGS) and Tangent-Guided Multi-Edge Projection (TGMP). It shares tangent spaces across CUDA blocks and amortizes overhead by generating and validating multiple edges in parallel along tangent directions.
sections.details:
The core idea of PATACON combines efficient tangent-space exploration (TGS) with reusing that search direction to generate and validate multiple edges at once on the GPU (TGMP).

### IV-A Tangent-Guided Sampling (TGS) for Parallel Search
Unlike standard RRT that samples the full ambient space, TGS samples search directions within the subspace $\mathcal{T}_r$ spanned by the null-space basis $N(q_r)$ at the tangent space origin $q_r$. This avoids steering in wasteful directions that pull far away from the manifold.
Tangent space data is stored in a "tangent-space bank" in GPU global memory, maintained separately for the start and goal trees. Each CUDA block dynamically pulls a ready tangent space from the bank, allowing blocks to explore different manifold regions in parallel without being tied to a fixed block.
When exploring a new tangent space, "backtracking prevention" is applied. By evaluating the inner product with the incoming direction from the parent tangent space, samples that steer backward into previously explored regions have their directions flipped, restricting exploration to the forward half-space. Nearest-neighbor searches are executed rapidly across nodes belonging to the selected tangent space via intra-block thread-parallel reductions.

### IV-B Tangent-Guided Multi-Edge Projection (TGMP)
Because building tangent spaces and searching nearest neighbors takes effort, advancing just one step per sample is inefficient on GPUs. TGMP generates a chain of up to $K_{\max}$ candidate nodes (set to 4 in experiments) along the chosen tangent direction with a fixed step size $\xi$.
However, since a tangent space is only a local linear approximation, stepping further away increases deviation from the actual manifold. The planner monitors the constraint error $E_M(\bar{q}_k) = \|h(\bar{q}_k)\|_2$ and truncates candidate generation once it exceeds a threshold $\epsilon_M$.

### IV-C Parallel Edge Projection and Validation on GPU
The generated candidate edges are assigned to cooperative thread groups within the CUDA block, where they are projected and validated concurrently on the GPU. Waypoints along an edge are projected sequentially, but the edges themselves are evaluated in parallel.
Results are checked in original sequential order, and only the longest continuous valid sequence from the root (Valid Prefix) is added to the tree. If a collision occurs or projection fails partway through, subsequent edges are discarded. A new tangent space is created and added to the bank only at the boundary node when all edges in a batch are accepted and the error threshold is exceeded.

### IV-D Connecting to the Opposing Tree and Bridge Validation (CONNECT)
Once an EXTEND step succeeds, the planner sets the nearest node in the opposing tree as a fixed target $q_{\mathrm{tar}}$ and enters the CONNECT phase to link the trees. It projects the direction vector toward the target onto the current tangent space and extends aggressively using TGMP.
To prevent numerical projection from pulling away from the target, a progress condition $\epsilon_{\mathrm{prog}}$ verifies that the distance to the target is strictly decreasing. Once both trees are sufficiently close, the final gap (bridge) is projected and checked for collisions; if valid, the path is complete.

captions.F2: GPU thread-mapping architecture of PATACON. Multiple CUDA blocks explore different tangent-space regions in parallel, and within each block, multiple generated candidate edges (Edges 0–3) are assigned to warps (32 threads) for concurrent validation.
captions.F3: Workflow of EXTEND and CONNECT in tangent space. In EXTEND, multiple candidate nodes are generated along the tangent direction until the error threshold is reached and projected onto the manifold. In CONNECT, the tree attempts repeated connections while projecting the direction toward the opposing target node onto the tangent space.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Dominance widens as dimensions and constraints grow!
sections.summary: Evaluated across eight environments ranging from a 7-DoF arm to a 35-DoF humanoid. While existing cpRRTC remains competitive in lower dimensions, PATACON achieved up to an 11.25 times speedup in higher-dimensional, tightly constrained tasks.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup and Benchmark Environments
Baselines included CPU SIMD-vectorized McVAMP, prior GPU-parallel projection planner cpRRTC, and sequential tangent-space planner TB-RRT. Experiments were conducted on a workstation equipped with an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D CPU and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU.
Five robot models were tested: (A) 7-DoF Franka Panda, (B) 14-DoF Dual Franka, (C) 15-DoF Fixed-base FFW-SG2, (D) 18-DoF Mobile FFW-SG2, and (E) 35-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid. Constraints evaluated included dual-arm relative pose constraints (BK: 6 DoF), end-effector orientation constraints (OR: 2 DoF), dual-foot contact constraints (FT: 12 DoF), and center-of-mass support polygon inequality constraints (CoM).

### V-B Performance Comparison Across Constraint Codimensions and Dimensions
Each task was evaluated across 100 random start and goal configurations. On the 7-DoF single-arm Franka, cpRRTC was faster because it did not incur tangent-space management overhead. However, as degrees of freedom and constraints increased, the balance shifted dramatically.
The difference was especially pronounced on the 15-DoF FFW-SG2 with both dual-arm closed-chain (BK) and end-effector orientation (OR) constraints. PATACON achieved an average planning time of around 0.026 seconds (throughput of ~38.5 plans per second), delivering an 11.25 times speedup over cpRRTC (~0.294 seconds, ~3.4 plans per second). In 35-DoF Unitree G1 whole-body planning, PATACON consistently maintained high success rates and low computation times, widening the gap over cpRRTC as constraints tightened.

### V-C Ablation Study of Proposed Components
Individual components were analyzed on the G1 whole-body task. Adding only Tangent-Guided Sampling (TGS) to cpRRTC made it slower due to the overhead of constructing tangent spaces. Adding multi-edge generation (TGMP) and processing edges sequentially began to amortize that cost. Validating multiple edges concurrently on the GPU as in PATACON, paired with backtracking prevention, substantially cut down execution time, highlighting the necessity of tightly coupling tangent-space geometry with GPU parallelization.

### V-D Anytime Optimization Behavior
PATACON's speed in finding an initial solution provides a major advantage in path optimization (anytime planning). Testing AO-PATACON—which updates cost bounds and re-explores trees whenever a solution is found—on the G1 humanoid showed that it reached 100% success within milliseconds of search start, and path length costs dropped steadily in a staircase fashion over a 10-second budget.

In higher-dimensional, tightly constrained settings (right columns and bottom row), PATACON (orange) reaches 100% success significantly further to the left (shorter time) than cpRRTC (green).

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: Pushing whole-body planning toward real time
sections.summary: By unifying a geometric approach using local tangent spaces with massively parallel GPU computing, PATACON proves that high-dimensional, tightly constrained motion planning can be drastically accelerated.
sections.details:
This work proposed PATACON, a GPU-parallel tangent-bundle RRT-Connect framework for constrained motion planning. By pairing a geometric formulation that explores along local tangent spaces with speculative multi-edge generation and parallel GPU validation, it successfully unlocks tangent-space planning on modern high-end GPUs—a class of methods that was previously difficult to parallelize.

Experiments on dual-arm manipulation and humanoid whole-body planning demonstrated that PATACON's advantage widens as dimensions and constraint tightness grow, achieving up to an 11.25 times speedup alongside high success rates. Generating whole-body trajectories within tens of milliseconds marks an important step toward true real-time whole-body planning, enabling continuous replanning while humanoids operate in dynamic real-world environments.

takeaways: When handling constraints in GPU-parallel RRT, steering along tangent spaces (tangent directions of the manifold) rather than blindly in ambient space drastically cuts wasted projections, offering a major speed advantage.
Constructing tangent spaces and performing nearest-neighbor queries adds overhead, but generating and validating multiple edges (TGMP) in parallel per sample on the GPU more than offsets the cost.

Simple GPU baselines like cpRRTC suffice for lower-dimensional problems with loose constraints, but PATACON clearly dominates in high-dimensional, tightly constrained tasks such as dual-arm with orientation constraints or humanoid whole-body planning (15–35 DoF).
limitations: In low-dimensional problems with loose constraints (such as a 7-DoF single arm), the cost of building and managing tangent spaces can outweigh the search reduction benefits, making it slower than simpler baselines.
Hyperparameters such as the tangent-space error threshold ($\epsilon_M$) and maximum step count ($K_{\max}$) may depend on the local curvature of the manifold and specific task geometry.
